content: 1. Gundersen JH and Nichols S reported on the early experiences with the large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) in patients with exocervical squamous intraepithelial lesions, highlighting its potential as a new approach to managing cervical lesions. (European Journal of Gynaecological Oncology, 1994) 2. Hallam NF et al. conducted a study involving 1,000 patients, demonstrating that LLETZ could serve as an alternative to local ablative treatments and cone biopsy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. (Journal of Gynecologic Surgery, 1993) 3. Haller H et al. examined the treatment outcomes of stage Ia1 squamous cell carcinoma of the uterine cervix, providing insights into effective management strategies. (International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics, 2011) 4. Hatch KD et al. explored the use of cryosurgery for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, emphasizing its role in the treatment of precancerous cervical lesions. (Obstetrics & Gynecology, 1981) 5. He S et al. investigated the utility of high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) testing for monitoring patients with high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia following cold-knife conization. (Chinese Journal of Clinical Oncology, 2011) 6. Hellberg D and Nilsson S shared their 20-year experience in following up abnormal cervical smears using colposcopy, histology, and treatment with conization or cryosurgery. (Gynecologic Oncology, 1990) 7. Hemmingsson E and Stenson S evaluated the long-term outcomes of cryosurgical treatment for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, with follow-up periods ranging from five to eight years. (American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology, 1981) 8. Herzog TJ et al. assessed the diagnostic and therapeutic potential of the cervical electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. (Gynecologic Oncology, 1995) 9. Hillemanns P et al. compared LEEP with cold-knife conization for the treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, highlighting differences in outcomes. (Zentralbl Gynakol, 2000) 10. Huang LW and Hwang JL compared the loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) and cold-knife conization in treating cervical dysplasia, focusing on residual disease in subsequent hysterectomy specimens. (Gynecologic Oncology, 1999) 11. Huchko MJ et al. evaluated the safety of LEEP performed by clinical officers in an HIV primary care setting, demonstrating its feasibility in resource-limited environments. (International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics, 2010) 12. Javaheri G et al. discussed the role of cryosurgery in treating intraepithelial neoplasia of the uterine cervix, emphasizing its effectiveness and safety. (Obstetrics & Gynecology, 1981) 13. Jones HW III and Buller RE reviewed the treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia using cone biopsy, providing a comprehensive analysis of its outcomes. (American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology, 1980) 14. Kamat AA et al. demonstrated the superiority of electrocautery over the suture method for achieving hemostasis in the cervical cone bed. (Obstetrics & Gynecology, 2003) 15. Kaufman RH and Irwin JF presented findings on the long-term follow-up of cryosurgical therapy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, emphasizing its durability. (American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology, 1978) 16. Keijser KG et al. highlighted the utility of diathermy loop excision in managing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, combining diagnosis and treatment in a single procedure. (American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology, 1992) 17. Kietpeerakool C et al. assessed the safety of LEEP in women with early invasive cervical carcinoma, confirming its efficacy in this patient population. (International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics, 2006) 18. Kreimer AR et al. demonstrated that HPV testing following LEEP identifies women at risk for post-treatment cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3. (Cancer Epidemiology, Biomarkers & Prevention, 2006) 19. Kristensen GB et al. conducted a randomized trial comparing cold-knife conization and laser conization, providing evidence for the relative benefits of each technique. (Obstetrics & Gynecology, 1990) 20. Larsson G et al. reported on the long-term follow-up of 1,013 women treated with conization for cervical dysplasia and carcinoma in situ, emphasizing the importance of monitoring. (Annales Chirurgiae et Gynaecologiae, 1981) 21. Luesley DM et al. examined the complications of cone biopsy related to cone dimensions and the influence of prior colposcopic assessment. (British Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology, 1985) 22. Mathévet P et al. compared three conization techniques—cold knife, laser, and LEEP—in a randomized prospective study, providing insights into their relative efficacy. (Gynecologic Oncology, 1994) 23. Mazouni C et al. evaluated the conservative treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia using a cold-knife section technique, highlighting its effectiveness. (European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, 2005) 24. Melnikow J et al. presented long-term follow-up data on cervical intraepithelial neoplasia outcomes after treatment, based on the British Columbia Cohort Study. (Journal of the National Cancer Institute, 2009) 25. Monaghan JM et al. discussed the use of colposcopically directed cryosurgery for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and its impact on subsequent pregnancy outcomes. (British Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology, 1982) 26. Nagai N et al. conducted a prospective study on HPV DNA status after loop excision for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade III, providing valuable prognostic information. (International Journal of Molecular Medicine, 2004) 27. Nene BM et al. evaluated the effectiveness, safety, and acceptability of cryotherapy performed by midwives for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in India. (International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics, 2008) 28. Ortolf G et al. reported that conization of the cervix increases perinatal mortality due to preterm delivery in subsequent pregnancies. (BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, 2010) 29. Prendiville W et al. introduced LLETZ as a new method for managing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, emphasizing its advantages in outpatient settings. (British Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology, 1989) 30. Reich O et al. provided long-term follow-up data on cervical intraepithelial neoplasia III after cold-knife conization with involved margins, highlighting recurrence risks.
